bib.title: How Much Knowledge Can You Pack Into the Parameters of a Language Model?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "How Much Knowledge Can You Pack Into the Parameters of a Language Model?", Adam Roberts*, Colin Raffel*, Noam Shazeer (Google; * equal contribution). Published in Proceedings of EMNLP 2020, pages 5418–5426, Nov 16–20, 2020 (the header is printed on page 1). arXiv 2002.08910.

COVERAGE: I read all 37,495 chars across 9 pages: abstract, sections 1–4, acknowledgments, references (skimmed for where the method comes from), Appendix A (NQ metrics) and Appendix B ("Other Things We Tried", which includes Fig. 2). Nothing was skipped. Page numbers below are PDF pages 1–9, which are proceedings pages 5418–5426.

CLAIMS
- claim: With no retrieval, the largest fine-tuned T5 + SSM is competitive with open-book (retrieve-then-read) systems. It reaches state of the art on WebQuestions and beats most baselines on NQ and TriviaQA.
  number: T5.1.1-XXL + SSM gives NQ 35.2, WQ 42.8, TQA dev 51.9, TQA test 61.6. Open-book comparisons: DPR (Karpukhin et al. 2020) 41.5 / 42.4 / 57.9 / –, and REALM (Guu et al. 2020) 40.4 / 40.7 / – / –.
  setup: Open-domain NQ (single-answer variant), WebQuestions and TriviaQA. Only the questions are used and all supplied documents are ignored. Exact match after normalisation. NQ and TQA are reported on dev sets, plus the official TQA test leaderboard (Wikipedia domain). Table 1 columns are NQ, WQ, TQA-dev, TQA-test.
  quote: "T5.1.1-XXL + SSM 35.2 42.8 51.9 61.6" / "Karpukhin et al. (2020) 41.5 42.4 57.9 –" / "T5.1.1- XXL with SSM ultimately achieves state-of-the-art on WebQuestions and our largest models beat most other methods on Natural Questions and TriviaQA. Importantly, all previous methods except Ling et al. (2020) and Févry et al. (2020) operate in the “open-book” setting"
  where: p.4, Table 1 and Results paragraph
  Caveat for the note: DPR (open-book) still beats the best closed-book model on NQ (41.5 vs 35.2) and TQA dev (57.9 vs 51.9). Closed-book wins only on WQ (42.8 vs 42.4).

- claim: Closed-book QA accuracy rises steadily with parameter count, Base (220M) through 11B.
  number: T5 Base→Large→3B→11B on NQ goes 25.9 → 28.5 → 30.4 → 32.6. On TQA dev it goes 23.8 → 28.7 → 35.1 → 42.3.
  setup: Original T5 checkpoints (multitask pre-trained on C4 span corruption plus supervised tasks). The T5.1.1 checkpoints are pre-trained on unlabeled data only and show the same trend (T5.1.1-Base 25.7 → XXL 32.8 on NQ).
  quote: "Base (220 million parameters), Large (770 million), 3B (3 billion), and 11B (11 billion)"; "performance on each dataset improves as the model size increases"; "T5-Base 25.9 27.9 23.8 29.1" ... "T5-11B 32.6 37.2 42.3 50.1"
  where: p.3 Training; p.4 Table 1

- claim: Continued pre-training with salient span masking (SSM, from REALM) gives a large boost. It masks one named entity or date per Wikipedia sentence and runs 100k extra steps.
  number: T5-11B goes from 32.6/37.2/42.3/50.1 to 34.8/40.8/51.0/60.5 with SSM.
  setup: Guu et al.'s BERT-mined Wikipedia salient-span sentences, used to continue pre-training T5 checkpoints for 100,000 steps before fine-tuning.
  quote: "continue pre-training the T5 checkpoints for 100,000 additional steps before fine-tuning"; "T5-11B + SSM 34.8 40.8 51.0 60.5"
  where: p.4 SSM paragraph, Table 1

- claim: The gain comes from the SSM objective, not from the dataset. Standard span corruption on the same sentences gives no significant gain.
  number: none
  setup: T5.1.1-XXL further pre-trained on Guu et al.'s Wikipedia sentences with SSM vs SC, fine-tuned on a mixture of the three QA tasks every 10k steps (Fig. 2).
  quote: "the SSM objective is clearly an important ingredient in the improved performance; we saw no significant improvement versus the baseline T5 model when using SC."
  where: p.9, Appendix B

- claim: Exact match undercounts a free-form generator. Of 150 NQ predictions scored wrong, only 62% were actually wrong. Adjusted accuracy is 57.8.
  number: 62.0% true negatives, 13.3% phrasing mismatch, 13.3% incomplete annotation, 11.3% unanswerable. Counts are 20/20/17 of 150. Adjusted score is 57.8.
  setup: Manual inspection of 150 NQ validation examples marked incorrect. The paper does not say which checkpoint was used; it says only "our model". The adjusted score removes unanswerable questions and applies the false-negative rate. The human-eval results are released.
  quote: "We found only 62% of these to be true positives." (Table 2 caption; the paper says "true positives" where it means "true negatives") / "20 were marked as incorrect due to differences in phrasing, another 20 were not annotated with all correct answers, and 17 were unanswerable without appropriate context. Removing unanswerable questions from the validation set and recomputing our model’s accuracy based on this false-negative rate produces a score of 57.8."
  where: p.5, Table 2 and Human Evaluation
  The authors concede open-book systems are affected too: "open-book question answering systems could also be impacted to a lesser extent by these issues" (p.5).

- claim: On the harder multi-answer NQ variant (official leaderboard style, recall only), closed-book T5 beats the original NQ baseline but trails oracle-context readers.
  number: T5-11B + SSM scores 36.2 recall, against 51.9 SOTA (Pan et al. 2019) and a 33.2 baseline.
  setup: NQ validation. The model outputs every answer delimited by "answer:". The comparison systems read the oracle context.
  quote: "T5-11B + SSM achieves a recall of 36.2 on the validation set, which lags behind the state-of-the-art score of 51.9 from Pan et al. (2019) but outperforms the best baseline published alongside the dataset (recall of 33.2"
  where: p.4

- claim: The authors argue closed-book skips retrieval and long-document reading, which saves compute and memory. The largest models are still costly.
  number: none
  quote: "most open-domain question answering systems must first do an expensive lookup step over the entire knowledge corpus and then attend to a long document to extract an answer. Our approach omits both of these steps"
  where: p.4

- claim: Negative results. Extra span-corruption pre-training on Wikipedia had "virtually no effect". Pre-training from scratch on Wikipedia only (up to 1T tokens) was "dramatically worse", which the authors suspect is overfitting. A multitask QA mix gave +0.5 on NQ but was slightly worse on the others. Sampling a random answer had no effect.
  number: 1 trillion tokens; +0.5 NQ
  quote: "We pre-trained on up to 1 trillion tokens ... this resulted in dramatically worse performance regardless of the amount of pre-training"; "multitask training improved performance on the Natural Questions by 0.5, it produced slightly worse results on the other tasks."
  where: p.8–9, Appendix B

- Training details: AdaFactor, constant LR 0.001, 10% dropout (5% for T5.1.1), batch 196,608 tokens, greedy decoding, 20,000 steps. Validation accuracy "typically plateaued after only a few hundred steps" (p.3–4).

LIMITS (the authors concede these in the Conclusion, p.5; this is the core material for a "why RAG" note):
- Cost: "we obtained state-of-the-art results only with the largest models which had around 11 billion parameters. This model size can be prohibitively expensive in resource-constrained settings"
- Provenance and hallucination: "“open-book” models typically provide some indication of what information they accessed when answering a question. This can provide a useful form of interpretability. In contrast, our model distributes knowledge in its parameters in an inexplicable way and hallucinates realistic-looking answers when it is unsure."
- Update and removal: "the maximum-likelihood objective used to train our model provides no guarantees as to whether a model will learn a fact or not. This makes it difficult to ensure that the model obtains specific knowledge over the course of pre-training and prevents us from explicitly updating or removing knowledge from a pre-trained model."
- Scope: the tasks "mainly measure “trivia”-style knowledge", with no reasoning or multi-hop tested (they point to DROP). Footnote 2 says they "do not directly address multi-hop inference".
- Time-dependence: the "unanswerable" category (e.g. "latest version of microsoft office", or the secretary of state for NI) shows that time-sensitive facts break parametric answers (p.5).
- What I noticed, not what the authors say: the scale is 2020-era (11B max), and the strongest baseline (DPR) still beats the paper on NQ and TQA. The comparison does not control for compute or for the retriever corpus. There is no test of hallucination rates or calibration beyond the qualitative statement.

BUILDS ON: Raffel et al. (2019) T5 / text-to-text; Guu et al. (2020) REALM, the source of salient span masking and its data; Petroni et al. (2019) "Language models as knowledge bases?"; Jiang et al. (2019); Talmor et al. (2019); Radford et al. (2019), zero-shot QA in GPT-2; Lee et al. (2019), the evaluation protocol and open-domain NQ; Shazeer and Stern (2018) Adafactor. Datasets are Kwiatkowski et al. (2019) NQ, Berant et al. (2013) WebQuestions and Joshi et al. (2017) TriviaQA. Concurrent closed-book work is Ling et al. (2020) RELIC and Févry et al. (2020) EAE. Prager (2006) is the source for the open-domain QA definition.

CODE: None in the paper. It points to released code and models at https://goo.gle/t5-cbqa (p.1) and human-eval data at https://goo.gle/t5-cbqa-human-eval (p.5). The multi-answer output format is "answer: John Lennon answer: Ringo Starr answer: George Harrison answer: Paul McCartney" (p.8).

FIGURES:
- Figure 1 (p.1): "T5 is pre-trained to fill in dropped-out spans of text (denoted by <M>) from documents in a large, unstructured text corpus. We fine-tune T5 to answer questions without inputting any additional information or context. This forces T5 to answer questions based on “knowledge” that it internalized during pre-training." This is the best candidate for the note. In one picture it shows parametric knowledge: pre-training as fill-in-the-blank, then "When was Franklin D. Roosevelt born? → 1882" with no context. It sets up the closed-book vs open-book contrast faster than prose.
- Figure 2 (p.9): SSM vs SC continued pre-training curves for T5.1.1-XXL. It is narrower and only useful if the note discusses pre-training objectives.
- Table 1 (p.4) is arguably the most useful visual for "why RAG". Closed-book T5 rows sit beside open-book REALM/DPR rows, and the scale trend is visible.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean. Ligatures (ﬁ) and a few accents (F´evry) are mangled but readable. Figure 1's text is jumbled in the extraction, and I took the caption from the caption text. Table 1's "dev test" header applies only to the TQA columns; I inferred this from the layout, which is consistent with the text saying NQ/TQA use dev sets plus a TQA test submission. The Table 2 caption says "true positives" where it means true negatives; that is the authors' wording, quoted as printed. The checkpoint behind the 57.8 human-eval score is not stated. There were no embedded instructions.
